Header:

- Duration: ~55m
- Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Reyes (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Zenex CTO), Liam O'Connell (Zenex Lead ML), María Gómez (Zenex Infra), Ethan Wu (Zenex SRE)

Auto-summary (auto gen - may be imperfect): Discussed KV cache thrash and eviction observed by Zenex when mixing long document context (>16k tokens) with interactive chat. SE explained cache sharding + prefix reuse effects. Actionables captured.

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate the time. This is Avery from Redwood, I'm the AE, with Jordan our systems SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Priya Rao: Doing well, thanks. Big thing for us is reproducible eviction causing latency spikes in prod, so we wanted to go deep.
[00:10] Jordan Reyes: Yep, thanks. Quick agenda: reproduce the eviction, go through cache architecture, paging behavior under long context, prefix reuse and hot-keying, then tactical mitigations and long-term remedies.
[00:18] Liam O'Connell: Sounds good. Quick context: we run a hybrid workload — 60% short chat (100-400 tokens), 40% long doc ingestion workflows (8k-30k tokens). We see intermittent 5-10s tail latency and some 429s during bursts.
[00:33] María Gómez: From infra side, the errors line up with high GPU memory churn, evictions appear correlated with serialized long-response generation.
[00:40] Jordan Reyes: Ok, that's consistent with KV paging. Some background: Redwood runtime keeps per-session KV slices in GPU memory for fast autoregressive decoding. We do continuous batching and try to keep active KV in LRU-ish caches, but mixing high sequence lengths blows up resident KV size.
[00:56] Ethan Wu: When you say LRU-ish, is that per-model or per-customer? We have multi-tenant pools.
[01:02] Jordan Reyes: Good question. By default we shard by routing key (customer + model + route) but with shared pools the physical caches are per-worker. So you can get eviction cross-talk between tenants unless you pin pools or use Dedicated.
[01:15] Priya Rao: We're on hosted for now but evaluating Private/VPC. If there's cross-tenant eviction that's a problem.
[01:21] Avery Chen: Right — Dedicated or Private gives you isolated GPU pools so you avoid noisy neighbor eviction. But we also recommended software-level mitigations.
[01:28] Liam O'Connell: Can you explain prefix reuse causing hits to drop? We saw hit rate degrade after we started reusing doc prefixes across sessions.
[01:36] Jordan Reyes: Sure, prefix reuse has two effects: it increases cache hit opportunities when the prefix is present, but if you have many similar prefixes with slight divergence, you create fragmentation: each unique KV entry consumes memory and replacement policy may evict other hot keys.
[01:48] Jordan Reyes: Also, we observed some customers inadvertently keep a long-running conversation open and repeatedly append different 2k token suffixes — that causes the KV per-session to grow linearly and evict other sessions.
[01:58] Priya Rao: That's exactly our pattern — analysts open a long doc session and kick off many small Q&A jobs from that context.
[02:04] Jordan Reyes: Right, so you get a pathological case: long-context sessions + high concurrency of short jobs referencing same prefix but with small diffs — net result is KV explosion.
[02:15] Avery Chen: Two classes of fixes: infra (Dedicated pools, pinning, per-customer cache partitions) and runtime (TTL/size caps per session, prefix compaction, proactive offload to CPU/SSD with paging).
[02:28] Liam O'Connell: Paging — how does that work? We saw references to paging to host memory and then to NVMe, but the latency numbers for paging were all over the place.
[02:37] Jordan Reyes: We have a multi-tier cache: GPU hot KV, then host RAM (pinned), then NVMe-backed cold store. Paging is synchronous on miss by default — which hurts latency. We can do async prefetching when we detect a pattern, but that adds complexity.
[02:52] María Gómez: Are there heuristics to prefetch for long reads? We have predictable read patterns for doc ingestion.
[02:56] Jordan Reyes: Yes, prefetch heuristics based on sequence length histogram and session reuse signals. For doc ingestion workflows we can treat the sequence as streaming and keep a sliding window pin so you avoid thrashing.
[03:06] Ethan Wu: Quantization — does it change eviction thresholds? We have customers using 4-bit quantized models to save memory.
[03:12] Jordan Reyes: Absolutely. Quantization reduces KV size per token in some kernels, but paired with mixed-precision kernels and attention caches, the memory savings aren't always linear. Also some quantized execution paths have different page sizes which affects fragmentation.
[03:25] Priya Rao: Ok, what about batching? Could batching short jobs help reduce eviction?
[03:29] Jordan Reyes: Batching helps throughput, but it increases peak memory as multiple sessions' KV are resident in the same worker during the batch. So batching can worsen eviction if you don't control per-worker max resident KV. Continuous batching + dynamic batch sizing by token count helps — limit batch by total KV tokens not just requests.
[03:45] Liam O'Connell: That makes sense. We're currently batching by request count only.
[03:49] Jordan Reyes: If you switch to token-budget batching you reduce peak memory and avoid surprising evictions.
[03:53] Priya Rao: Any quick instrument we should add to our telemetry?
[03:57] Jordan Reyes: Track per-session KV size, per-worker aggregate KV resident size, eviction rate, and time-to-page (GPU->CPU and CPU->NVMe). Also correlate with 95th/99th latency by route.
[04:09] Avery Chen: We'll share a sample Prometheus dashboard and the repro script.
[04:13] Priya Rao: Great. Can you walk through repro steps now?
[04:16] Jordan Reyes: Sure. We usually do: 1) create long-session with streaming ingestion ~20k tokens, 2) spin up 20 parallel short Q&A calls referencing that session, 3) observe per-worker KV growth and eviction; we also toggle batching and token-budget limits to compare. I'll share the script.
[04:30] Liam O'Connell: When eviction happens, where do tokens go? Are they evicted completely or partially evicted from the attention KV?
[04:36] Jordan Reyes: We evict whole KV value entries at shard granularity. Attention states are chunked by layer and head; eviction removes the entire chunk, which causes recomputation or page-in on next request. That recompute costs latency.
[04:48] María Gómez: Is recompute cheaper than background paging?
[04:51] Jordan Reyes: Depends. For short reaccess, recompute can be cheaper than async NVMe page-in because recompute uses GPU cycles but avoids I/O. For large contexts, paging is better but you need fast NVMe and prefetching.
[05:03] Ethan Wu: Any knobs for TTLs? We want to avoid long sessions monopolizing cache.
[05:07] Jordan Reyes: We support per-route TTLs and max-kv-bytes per-session. You can set low TTL for interactive chat flows and higher caps for ingestion routes. Also there's a pinning API to mark certain prefixes as critical (hot-key pinning).
[05:20] Priya Rao: Is pinning safe in multi-tenant pools? Could pinning starve others?
[05:23] Jordan Reyes: It can if you don't cap pinned memory; in shared pools we recommend pinned-per-customer limits and admission control. That's one reason Dedicated is simpler.
[05:33] Avery Chen: Quick question for Zenex infra: what's your current worker pool size and per-worker GPU memory?
[05:38] María Gómez: We're on a 4-node pool with A100s (80GB) but we run about 6 workers per GPU to increase utilization.
[05:46] Jordan Reyes: Running 6 workers per 80GB may be aggressive for mixed long-context workloads; you'd want fewer workers or bigger instance types for those flows.
[05:55] Liam O'Connell: So runner counts + batching + token budget all interplay. If we reduce workers per GPU and increase token budgets, do we trade cost for tail latency stability?
[06:05] Jordan Reyes: Yes, it's a tradeoff. We can model expected resident KV given your seq distribution. I'll run a quick estimation with your numbers after the call.
[06:12] Priya Rao: Let's talk about prefix reuse mitigation — any server-side compaction?
[06:16] Jordan Reyes: We have prefix compaction that deduplicates identical KV blocks across sessions when the routing key indicates the same canonical prefix. But compaction is CPU-intensive and best done offline or as low-priority background job.
[06:28] Priya Rao: Our issue seems to be near-identical prefixes — small diffs. Compaction won't help much there.
[06:33] Jordan Reyes: Correct; in those cases you'd want logical session splits or summarization — summarize long context into a condensed embedding/summary and use that as prefix to keep KV small.
[06:44] Liam O'Connell: Any impact from model architecture? Different models have different KV growth per token?
[06:48] Jordan Reyes: Yes — decoder-only transformers have more KV per token compared to some optimized architectures with key-value compression. Also number of layers, heads, and kv projection sizes directly change memory. We'll include model-specific guidance in the doc.
[07:00] María Gómez: About NVMe — we can provision hot NVMe on our nodes; what's recommended latency for acceptable page-in?
[07:06] Jordan Reyes: For practical purposes, aim for sub-2ms NVMe reads and low host->GPU PCIe transfer overhead. If page-in end-to-end is >20ms you'll see user-visible spikes. Prefetching can help hide that but requires predictable access patterns.
[07:20] Priya Rao: For Private/VPC, is there a recommended cluster topology?
[07:24] Avery Chen: For Zenex's mix, we usually suggest two classes of pools: heavy long-context pools with fewer workers per GPU and short-chat pools optimized for high concurrency. Route requests by model/route to the appropriate pool.
[07:36] Liam O'Connell: That routing is at the Redwood smart router layer?
[07:39] Jordan Reyes: Yes, routing policies can go by latency SLO, sequence length hint, or customer tier. You can also do automatic fallback to a more compute-heavy model when capacity constraints hit.
[07:50] Ethan Wu: About debugging — any logs/metrics we should pull? You mentioned per-worker resident KV, eviction events, page-in latencies. Anything else?
[07:57] Jordan Reyes: Also capture GPU memory alloc trace, batch composition over time (token counts per batch), and per-request KV footprint. We'll provide a script to annotate logs with request IDs so you can correlate.
[08:10] Priya Rao: Can we do a short live repro now? We can't expose prod traffic but maybe an emulated run.
[08:15] Avery Chen: We can run the repro against a sandbox; Jordan has a script. Jordan, do you want to share parameters so Zenex can run it?
[08:20] Jordan Reyes: Yep: choose seq lengths [20k ingest], short queries 100-300 tokens, concurrency 20, batch token budget 40k, workers-per-gpu 6. Toggle batch-vs-token-budget and observe per-worker GW and evictions. I'll drop the script in the doc.
[08:37] Liam O'Connell: One more operational ask — is there an API to evict or flush session KV manually?
[08:41] Jordan Reyes: Yes: session flush and per-route flush APIs exist. We also have a soft-evict that marks sessions for eviction after current request finishes to avoid mid-request recompute.
[08:52] María Gómez: What's the cost model for Dedicated vs Hosted if we move to dedicated pools?
[08:56] Avery Chen: Pricing depends on committed capacity; Dedicated is monthly reserved capacity with breakouts by GPU type. I'll share pricing but in short, Dedicated reduces noisy neighbor risk at predictable monthly cost.
[09:07] Priya Rao: Let's recap next steps.
[09:10] Avery Chen: Jordan will share repro script and dashboard; I'll send SOC2 and network diagram; Zenex team will run repro in sandbox and provide logs plus sequence histograms. We'll reconvene after the repro.
[09:20] Priya Rao: Thanks all, that was really helpful.
[09:23] Avery Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email.

(Transcript end; auto-transcription notes: occasional mis-heard product names: 'Redwood Dedicated' sometimes transcribed as 'Redwood Dedicatede', 'KV' sometimes 'kay-vee'. Timestamps approximate.)
